chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I said to him, 'A man became ill and left the optional prayers.' He said, 'O Muhammad, it is not an obligation. If he fulfills it, it is better for him to do so; and if he does not do it, there is nothing upon him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on optional prayers for a sick person who misses them?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam Muhammad al-Baqir (or al-Sadih, depending on the specific chain interpretation, but typically attributed to the Imams in this context) clarifies the status of *nafl* (voluntary) prayers for the ill, distinguishing them from *fard* (obligatory) prayers. The ruling emphasizes that while performing them is a virtuous act (*khayr*), their omission due to illness carries no penalty (*la shay' alayhi*), reflecting the Shia principle of ease (*taysir*) in worship during hardship. This highlights the juristic distinction between the strict obligation of *fard* and the recommended nature of *nafl*, where sickness serves as a valid excuse for non-performance without requiring later makeup (*qada*) unless one chooses to do so.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hareyz Bin Muslim who said,

‘I said to himasws, ‘A man is sick, so he leaves the optional (Salāts)’. So heasws said: ‘O Muhammad! It is not an Obligation that he should be fulfilling it. If it better if he does it, but if he does not do it, so there is nothing upon him’.
en.sarwar: 5. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from Hammad, from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim who has said the following:

“I once said to him (the Imam), ‘Alayhi al-Salam, ‘There is a man who has become ill and has omitted optional Salah (prayer).’ He (the Imam) said, ‘O Muhammad, it is not obligatory Salah (prayer). If he performs, it is a good deed that he does. If he did not do, he is not required to perform it.’”
